newsitem.title: CHINA: China must enforce IPR rules - business officials.
newsitem.headline: China must enforce IPR rules - business officials.

text.p: Foreign business executives said on Tuesday that China needed to do more to protect copyrights and other intellectual property and called for closer cooperation with Chinese government bodies.

But a member of a Chinese government think-tank said proper enforcement and education could take years, despite the 1995 intellectual property rights (IPR) protection agreement with the United States and China's acceptance of other international conventions.

"There are still a number of areas where Chinese compliance with intellectual property rights needs to improve," said Myron Brilliant, director of trade policy and Asian affairs for the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.
"There has been progress by the Chinese because they have closed down a lot of the CD factories, but a big component is border enforcement," Brilliant said.

Brilliant, speaking at a forum organised by the world business organisation, the International Chamber of Commerce, said the bilateral agreement had also failed to tackle some key issues including patents protection.
These would have to be addressed during negotiations for China's World Trade Organisation (WTO) membership, he added.
"The laws are in place to deal with counterfeiting, it's a question of mobilising," said Robert Miller, vice president of general counsel and public affairs for Procter & Gamble Asia.
The U.S.-based firm, which is a major seller of consumer products in China, has uncovered fakes emulating just about all of its main items, he said.

Despite the two-year-old Sino-U.S. agreement on protection of IPR and the closure of many factories, pirated products of all sorts -- from tea bags to video disks -- remain hot sellers throughout China.

Zheng Chengsi, director of the official Chinese Academy of Social Sciences' intellectual property centre, told the forum he believed enforcement would improve with the help of China's new Criminal Law, promulgated in March.

The law prescribes prison sentences of up to seven years as well as fines for stealing intellectual property, Zheng said. But the officials who were supposed to be enforcing the laws often did not understand them, he said.
"The big problem is that we've just started to protect intellectual property rights for the last 10 years or so," Zheng said.
"Frequently, lawyers and courts don't understand...so the important thing is to let everyone know what intellectual property is," he said.

Procter & Gamble's Miller suggested the Chinese government go a step further by collaborating more closely with private business, which could provide both education and funding to help China better understand IPR protection.
"We've seen progress, but I would offer that there is room to collaborate," he said.
Joseph Villella, assistant general counsel of intellectual property and licensing for IBM Asia Pacific, said one way to reduce piracy was to form joint ventures with Chinese partners.
